2. Sensor alerts from an Iceberg table

Say you look after a plant's temperature sensors. When a machine runs hot for three minutes in a row, someone on call gets paged, and if the alert is wrong in either direction, it's their night or the machine that pays for it. You want an alert at every reading that is the third or more in a row above 30 °C. The sensors write a reading per device per minute to an Iceberg table, and the rule is iot-consecutive-threshold in the query catalogue (Azure Stream Analytics' MATCH_RECOGNIZE example). In SQL that is two LAGs over a window. Window queries are where engines disagree, and we'll run into three causes:
  • ties: two readings of a device at the same instant make "previous reading" ambiguous, and each engine picks one;
  • NaN: a glitching sensor sends NaN. In SQL NaN > 30 is TRUE, because NaN sorts above every number, and in Python and pandas it is False, so a prototype and the production job disagree;
  • warehouses without row order: Snowflake and Spark tables have no order to break ties with.
As in the first notebook, the job reads the source, states and proves a contract, runs on several engines, keeps up with new data and writes a sink.

1. The source: an Iceberg table of readings

Iceberg needs a catalog, so a small SQLite one in a temporary folder stands in for Glue, a REST catalog or Unity. device_id and ts are required. Device 2 skipped a reading (NULL), and device 3 had a glitch and sent NaN. We'll see what each does to the alerts.

data.text/markdown:
2. The rule, and the first thing the checker says

Straight from the catalogue, three high readings in a row:

Whoever gets paged at 3 a.m. assumes that every alert means the temperature is above 30 and that one hot minute pages them once. We'll write both down and ask the checker, first with no assumptions about the input:

NOT proved: 1 of 2 postconditions not proved
⚠️ rows may tie in the ORDER BY of a window, of a LIMIT or of first(), last(), group_concat(), mode(), argmin() or argmax(), so the engine decides their order and a rerun may give other rows. The postconditions are proved for every order (LAG(temperature, 1, NULL), LAG(temperature, 2, NULL) over rows that tie in PARTITION BY [device_id] ORDER BY [ts], with no key among those columns). For a reproducible result, declare unique(device_id, ts) in the requires of 'readings' semantics: reference
postcondition status
(_.temperature > 30) ✅ proved
unique(device_id, ts) ❌ the preconditions do not make it a key: device_id, ts come from readings.device_id, readings.ts: declare sv.unique('device_id', 'ts') in the requires of 'readings'
output column known values
device_id any integer
ts any timestamp
temperature a double > 30.0

temperature > 30 is proved: it holds whichever reading the engine takes as the previous one. One alert per device and minute is not, and the report warns that the result is not deterministic. If a device can send two readings with the same ts, which one is "previous" depends on how the engine breaks the tie, and a rerun may page you twice. The catalogue found this in 44 of its 139 queries (dedup, top-N, LAG over equal timestamps; see its findings), and it is the most common way for engines to disagree. The fix is to state what the source promises: at most one reading per device and minute. The sensor team can make that promise, and the job checks it on every batch.

3. The NaN glitch

With that key we try again, and also ask that no alert is a NaN, since the person paged needs a temperature:

NOT proved: 1 of 3 postconditions not proved
semantics: reference
postcondition status
(_.temperature > 30) ✅ proved
~_.temperature.isnan() ❌ it may be FALSE on some rows
unique(device_id, ts) ✅ proved
output column known values
device_id any integer
ts any timestamp
temperature a double > 30.0

temperature > 30 and the key are proved now. The checker refuses ~isnan() rightly: in SQL NaN > 30 is TRUE, since NaN sorts above every number, so device 3's glitch counts as hot and pages someone. Python says the opposite, which is how a rule tested in pandas misbehaves in the warehouse:
So we define a high reading to exclude NaN. NaN then breaks the run, as a missing reading does:

data.text/markdown:
5. Every engine, and the warehouses

The alerts may run on a laptop today and in a warehouse tomorrow. DuckDB (Tier 1), Polars and DataFusion run the checked plan with the same rows, whichever engine= the node is refreshed with. Snowflake and Spark tables have no row order, so sverify refuses to write a window for them unless you promise that the order keys have no ties. The report's deterministic is that promise, proved from the key, so it can be passed on:

data.text/html: "Snowflake tables have no row order, so FETCH and windows over a named table cannot follow the Lean model's list order (windows run with deterministic=True)"

data.text/markdown:
With deterministic=True the SQL is written. Without the key, deterministic would be False, and passing deterministic=True anyway would be an unproved promise.

6. New readings, and a sensor that sends twice

Windows aren't incrementally maintained yet, and the node says so. A node like this is recomputed and diffed on each refresh, and its change still flows to the sink and to nodes downstream:

console.name: stdout
console.text: alerts: readings@v1; touched groups recomputed (no delta rules: not incrementally maintainable (left join, fetch or window))

data.text/markdown: We store the node in an Iceberg sink with .write, and its first refresh writes the first state. The sink keeps the contract in the table properties and in every snapshot summary:

data.text/markdown: Device 2's 12:03 reading doesn't alert because 12:01 was missing; 12:04 does. Then device 1 sends two readings for 12:04. The key rules out exactly this case, which would make the alerts depend on the engine. The refresh refuses the batch and changes nothing: the node and the sink stay at the last good version, and the next refresh retries from there.

data.text/markdown:
What you got

You now have alerts the on-call engineer can rely on. The checker found two bugs before anything ran, an alert that depended on how ties were broken and a NaN reading that would have paged someone. The key is checked on every batch, so a sensor that sends twice stops the job and leaves the alerts as they were. The same plan runs on DuckDB, Polars and DataFusion, and Snowflake or Spark SQL is written once the tie-freedom it needs is proved. The window node says it isn't incremental and stays up to date by recomputation, with its change written to the sink. Next up: An orders mart in SQL and Ibis, where a dashboard's dbt tests become a contract. Contracts covers windows, ties and the other double semantics in depth.
